mcqs.q: Communication is best defined as a process by which we:
opts: Allocate and convey meanings to create shared understanding
mcqs.explain: Communication is the process by which we allocate and convey meanings in an attempt to create shared understanding with others.

mcqs.q: The two broad types of communication are:
mcqs.explain: Communication is classified as verbal (conversation, words, voice) and non-verbal (body movements and facial expressions).

mcqs.q: Which is an element of VERBAL communication?
opts: Choice of words and voice control
mcqs.explain: Verbal communication involves the style & matter of conversation, choice of words, and voice control; smiles/eyebrows/frowning are non-verbal.

mcqs.q: Non-verbal communication includes:
mcqs.explain: Non-verbal communication involves a range of bodily movements and facial expressions such as smiling, raised eyebrows and frowning.

mcqs.q: Which is NOT one of the five components of communication?
mcqs.explain: The five components are Sender, Receiver, Message, Channels of communication, and Feedback. ‘Diagnosis’ is not one of them.

mcqs.q: The element that lets the sender know the message was understood is the:
mcqs.explain: Feedback is the response that closes the loop and indicates whether the message achieved shared understanding.

mcqs.q: The first step in any consultation about health behavior change should be to:
opts: Create a good rapport / constructive relationship with the patient
Hand the patient a leaflet and leave
mcqs.explain: The first step is to create good ‘rapport’ — a constructive relationship — because the quality of the relationship correlates with behavior-change outcomes.

mcqs.q: Rapport is important because the quality of the clinician–patient relationship correlates with:
mcqs.explain: The quality of the relationship between clinician and patient correlates with patient behavior-change outcomes.

mcqs.q: Which helps create good rapport with patients?
opts: Smiling, welcoming them, and taking time to listen
mcqs.explain: Building rapport: smile and welcome patients, mind the non-verbals, time your questions, listen, and make them comfortable to return.

mcqs.q: The three styles of clinical communication are:
mcqs.explain: Clinicians communicate using a directing, guiding, or following style, switching flexibly between them.

mcqs.q: The DIRECTING style of communication is:
opts: Delivery of expert advice & help — the traditional dominant approach
mcqs.explain: Directing = delivery of expert advice and help; traditionally the dominant health-care approach, best employed where rapport is already good.

mcqs.q: A FOLLOWING style is most appropriate when:
opts: Sensitivity is required, e.g. the patient is upset or you are breaking bad news
You must give detailed technical instructions fast
The patient asks for a fact
Rapport is already excellent and advice is wanted
mcqs.explain: Following uses listening skills in situations needing sensitivity; the goal is support and encouragement, not solving the problem immediately.

mcqs.q: The GUIDING style is most appropriate for:
opts: Talking about behavior change, especially with ambivalent patients
mcqs.explain: In guiding, clinician and patient work together so the patient identifies their own goals — most appropriate for behavior change, especially with ambivalent patients.

mcqs.q: Skilled clinical communication mainly involves:
opts: Identifying which style suits the moment and switching flexibly between styles
Always using a single fixed style
mcqs.explain: Skill is in identifying which communication style is best suited to a given point in the visit and switching flexibly between them.

mcqs.q: Deciding to talk about behavior change should ultimately be:
opts: The patient's choice — this lowers resistance
mcqs.explain: Letting the patient choose to discuss change increases their feeling of personal freedom and, in turn, lowers resistance.

mcqs.q: OPEN questions are valuable because they:
opts: Encourage the patient to explore feelings and give a deeper understanding
mcqs.explain: Open questions encourage the patient to explore how they feel and help the clinician gain a deeper understanding of the patient's views.

mcqs.q: A limitation of CLOSED questions is that they:
mcqs.explain: Closed questions only give limited information, making it harder for the clinician to deduce clinically relevant information.

mcqs.q: Statements that show appreciation for a patient's efforts and reinforce positive acts are called:
mcqs.explain: Affirmations demonstrate appreciation for the patient's efforts and help them believe in their ability to change / reinforce positive acts.

mcqs.q: Reflective listening is best described as:
opts: Making a statement in reply to what the patient said to demonstrate understanding
mcqs.explain: Reflective listening turns passive hearing into an active process by making a statement in reply that demonstrates understanding.

mcqs.q: Compared with ordinary listening, reflective listening is:
opts: An active process in which the listener checks understanding
mcqs.explain: Ordinary listening is passive; unless the listener checks what was understood, accurate understanding cannot be assumed — so listening must be active.

mcqs.q: Which is one of the TWO functions of reflective listening?
opts: It lets the listener check what they understood from the speaker
It replaces the need for rapport
mcqs.explain: Reflective listening (1) lets the listener check understanding and (2) makes the speaker feel understood, enhancing rapport and encouraging elaboration.

mcqs.q: A second function of reflective listening is that it makes the speaker:
opts: Feel understood and encourages them to elaborate
mcqs.explain: It enables the speaker to feel understood (enhancing rapport) and encourages them to elaborate and give more detail.

mcqs.q: Why is giving ‘redundant’ information a problem?
opts: Telling patients what they already know wastes precious time
mcqs.explain: Time is precious; telling the patient things they already know is a waste of that time.

mcqs.q: For information to be effective it should:
opts: Add to existing knowledge and feel personally relevant to the patient
Be as long and detailed as possible
Repeat what the patient already knows
mcqs.explain: Effective information needs to add to the patient's existing knowledge and be seen as personally relevant.

mcqs.q: The three steps of the Elicit–Provide–Elicit method are:
opts: Assess what the patient knows → provide information → elicit what it means to them
mcqs.explain: Elicit (assess what the patient already knows) → Provide (further information) → Elicit (what the information means for the patient).

mcqs.q: The FIRST step of the Elicit–Provide–Elicit method is to:
opts: Assess what the patient already knows
Provide all the information at once
mcqs.explain: It begins by eliciting/assessing what the patient already knows, before providing new information.

mcqs.q: A ‘collecting’ summary is one that:
opts: Brings together the key issues the patient raised
mcqs.explain: A collecting summary brings together the key issues raised by the patient.

mcqs.q: A summary used to close a session or move the discussion on is a:
mcqs.explain: A wrapping-up summary is used to close a session or move the discussion on; collecting and linking summaries serve other roles.

mcqs.q: Barriers to communication are classified into which four groups?
mcqs.explain: Communication barriers are psychological, physiological, environmental and cultural.

mcqs.q: Background noise and lack of privacy in the clinic are which type of communication barrier?
mcqs.explain: Noise, distractions and lack of privacy are environmental barriers; fear/anxiety are psychological, pain/hearing loss are physiological, language/beliefs are cultural.

saqs.q: Define communication and list its five components.
saqs.a: Communication is the process by which we allocate & convey meanings to create shared understanding. Five components: Sender, Receiver, Message, Channels of communication, Feedback.

saqs.q: Name the two types of communication and give an example of each.
saqs.a: Verbal — style/matter of conversation, choice of words, voice control. Non-verbal — bodily movements & facial expressions (smile, raised eyebrows, frowning).

saqs.q: Describe the three styles of clinical communication and when each is used.
saqs.a: Directing = giving expert advice/help (best when rapport is good). Following = listening & support where sensitivity is needed (e.g. upset patient / bad news), not solving immediately. Guiding = working together so the patient finds their own goals — best for behavior change & ambivalent patients.

saqs.q: What is reflective listening and what are its two functions?
saqs.a: Reflective listening = making a statement in reply to what the patient said to demonstrate understanding (active, not passive). Functions: 1) it lets the listener check what they understood; 2) it makes the speaker feel understood (enhancing rapport) and encourages them to elaborate.

saqs.q: Describe the Elicit–Provide–Elicit method and name the three types of summary.
saqs.a: Elicit–Provide–Elicit: assess what the patient already knows → provide further information → elicit what the information means for them. Three summaries: collecting (key issues), linking (links what was said), wrapping-up (close/move on).

saqs.q: List the four categories of barriers to communication.
saqs.a: Psychological (fear, anxiety, anger), Physiological (pain, hearing/speech impairment, fatigue), Environmental (noise, lack of privacy), and Cultural (language, beliefs, customs).
